statements.claim: The defeated suitors gathered in Bhishmaka's assembly hall in Kundina after Krishna carried off Rukmini from the swayamvara, before scattering to their kingdoms.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109 opens with the kings, anxious to go to their kingdoms, returning to Bhishmaka's assembly-hall after Vasudeva's son's departure; Rukmini context carried from corpus chain (DKS_0158).

statements.claim: Bhishmaka, well read in the laws of conduct, asked the kings' forgiveness for the fruit of his misconduct.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109: 'king Bhishmaka, the foremost of kings and well-read in moral laws... Do you forgive me for the fruit that is the outcome of my misconduct'.

statements.claim: Bhishmaka sent away the monarchs of Central India and of the east, west, and north, who departed delighted; the circle remaining included Jarasandha, Sunitha, Dantavakra, Shalya of Soubha, Mahakurma, Kaishika, the Pravara kings, Venudari, the king of Kashmir, and the kings of the Deccan.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109 lists exactly these kings remaining 'desirous of listening to the mystery' after the others went away delightedly.

statements.claim: Bhishmaka spoke of his son with fear, praising Krishna as foremost of beings and blessing Devaki who conceived the lotus-eyed Krishna.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109: 'Observing the movements of my son my eyes are agitated with fear... Blessed is Devaki... who has conceived as her son the lotus-eyed Krishna'.

statements.claim: Shalya counselled: Kshatriyas meet success or defeat in battle; save Baladeva and Krishna no third person can withstand Bhishmaka's son, who handles the Bhargava weapons.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109 (19-23): exact parallel of Shalya's speech.

statements.claim: Shalya said even the holder of the trident (Siva) cannot defeat Krishna in this land, and that Bhishmaka's son, knowing Keshava as Ishana, did not engage in fight with him.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109 (24-25): 'In this land of mortals even the holder of trident (Siva) cannot defeat him... Knowing Keshava as Ishāna he did not engage in fight with him'.

statements.claim: Gargya, desiring a son, adored Rudra for twelve years living on powdered iron; Rudra granted a boon that his son would be unslayable by the kings of Mathura.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109 (26-29): Gārgya's twelve-year penance on powdered iron and the boon that the kings of Mathurā could not slay his son.

statements.claim: By that boon Kalayavana is unslayable by the kings of Mathura in the battlefield and especially in the city of Mathura, and could defeat Krishna if they fought.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109 (29-30): 'Kālayavana is unslayable by the kings of Mathura in the battle-field and especially in the city of Mathurā... if he comes to battle and fights with him he will be able to defeat him'.

statements.claim: Shalya urged the kings to send an emissary to the capital of the king of the Yavanas; the delighted kings agreed, while Jarasandha lost heart recollecting the words of Brahma and lamented that the chiefs now made him seek another's shelter.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109 (32-35): kings say 'We will do it'; Jarāsandha 'lost heart' and gave the damsel/stranger lament.

statements.claim: Jarasandha dispatched Shalya of Soubha as envoy to the capital of the Yavanas.
statements.evidence: Index summary: 'Jarasandha dispatches Shalya as envoy'; excerpt: 'This effulgent king of Soubha... let him proceed to the capital of Yavana'; continued in DKS_0160.

notes: Highly faithful to HV 1.109; dialogue rendered nearly verbatim. Opening Rukmini-swayamvara framing is chain context from DKS_0158, not contradicted by pack.

statements.claim: A cold, fragrant, delightful wind blew in the Yavana capital and the assembled Yavanas wondered whence it came, then saw a car coming from the south.
statements.evidence: HV 1.110 (2-6): 'there blew delightful, but exciting, cold and fragrant wind... Whence it has come?... they saw a car coming from the south'.

statements.claim: Kalayavana governed his city in pursuance of royal duties, being wise, conversant with the threefold objects, proficient in policy, innocent of the sevenfold calamities, endued with accomplishments, versed in scriptures, pious, truthful, master of his senses, acquainted with war, expert in capturing forts, heroic, and honoring his ministers.
statements.evidence: HV 1.110 (1): nearly verbatim catalogue of Kalayavana's virtues.

statements.claim: Kalayavana sat at ease encircled by ministers while learned Yavanas discoursing on celestial themes adored him.

The car was golden and white, lit with jewels, adorned with celestial flags and pennons, drawn by horses fleet like mind or air, decked with tiger-skins, built by the celestial Architect, effulgent like the sun; the powerful and beautiful king of Soubha, Shalya, sat on it.
statements.evidence: HV 1.110 (7-12): full description matches, including 'constructed by the celestial Architect'.

statements.claim: Delighted at seeing his friend, Kalayavana sent for arghya and water for washing the feet, rose from his throne, and waited at the landing stair of the car.

Shalya descended alone with a confident heart and joyously entered the Yavana palace, but refused the arghya, saying he was an envoy of the kings dispatched by Jarasandha and did not deserve arghya from the kings.
statements.evidence: HV 1.110 (15-18): Shalya's refusal speech quoted almost verbatim.

statements.claim: Kalayavana replied that he knew Shalya was sent by the king of Magadha for the kings' behalf, that by adoring Shalya he worshipped the whole host of kings, and asked him to sit on the throne.

They shook hands, enquired of each other's welfare, and sat at ease on the sacred throne; Kalayavana asked what had become impossible for the king on whose arm-strength the kings lived without anxiety, and promised to carry out even a very difficult mandate.

Shalya delivered Jarasandha's message: Krishna oppressed the world from birth; Jarasandha, with kings and fourfold forces, besieged mount Gomanta, set fire to it at the king of Chedi's words; Rama leaped down with the golden-hilted sword, slaughtered the army, ground elephants, horses and soldiers with his ploughshare and mace, and destroyed elephants with elephants, cars with cars, cavalry with horses.
statements.evidence: HV 1.110 (26-33): full battle narration matches in detail.

statements.claim: Krishna then leaped down with his sun-bright discus and black iron club, shaking the mountain, and the mountain, whirled and bathed with shower, extinguished the fire and entered the earth as if dancing.
The mandate ended with the plea to 'enter the city of Mathura with your army and establish your glory there'.
statements.evidence: Index excerpt of HV 1.110: 'enter the city of Mathurā with your army establish your glory there'.

notes: Faithful retelling of HV 1.110; Jarasandha's Gomanta speech reproduced nearly verbatim. No unsupported factual claims.

statements.claim: Kalayavana rejoiced that numberless kings had requested him to vanquish Krishna, whom he called invincible in the three worlds even unto gods and Asuras, and declared he would start for Mathura that very day to defeat Keshava in the battlefield.
statements.evidence: HV 1.111 (1-6): Kalayavana's elated speech, including 'in this auspicious moment I shall even to-day start for Mathurā for defeating Keshava in the battle-field'.

statements.claim: Kalayavana said even his discomfiture in the task would be tantamount to success and he would carry out Emperor Jarasandha's command issued at the kings' request.
statements.evidence: HV 1.111 (5): 'Even my discomfiture in it will be, tantamount to my success... I shall carry out the command of the Emperor Jarasandha issued at the request of the kings'.

statements.claim: Kalayavana honored Shalya with highly precious gems and dresses, gave away riches to his guest and the Brahmanas, offered libations to fire, and after benedictory rites set out with his army to vanquish Janarddana.
Shalya, his desire fully achieved, embraced the lord of the Yavanas and set out with a delighted heart for his own city, carrying the answer back to the kings.
statements.evidence: HV 1.111 (10); the 'answer' is a reasonable connective inference consistent with the narrative.

statements.claim: Gargya, called impotent by his brother-in-law in an assembly of the Yadavas, was offended by their laughter and repaired to the shores of the western sea to do penance for a son who should be a terror to the tribe of Yadu.
statements.evidence: VP 5.23: 'Śyála having called Gárgya the Brahman... impotent, in an assembly of the Yádavas, they all laughed; at which he was highly offended, and repaired to the shores of the western sea'.

statements.claim: For twelve years Gargya propitiated Mahadeva living on iron sand, and the deity gave him the desired boon; the childless Yavana king befriended him, and Gargya begot by the king's wife a son as black as a bee, with a breast hard as the thunderbolt, called Kalayavana.
statements.evidence: VP 5.23: penance on iron sand for twelve years, son 'as black as a bee... breast was as hard as the point of the thunderbolt... thence called Kálayavana'.

statements.claim: The old Yavana king placed Kalayavana on the throne and retired to the woods; Kalayavana asked Narada who were the most mighty heroes on earth and was answered: 'The Yadavas'.
statements.evidence: VP 5.23: 'The Yavana king having placed his son... upon the throne, retired to the woods... demanded of Nárada who were the most mighty heroes on earth. To which the sage answered, The Yádavas'.

statements.claim: Kalayavana assembled many myriads of Mlechchhas and barbarians and advanced impatiently against Mathura with elephants, cavalry, chariots and foot, wearying his animal daily but insensible of fatigue himself.
statements.evidence: VP 5.23: 'assembled many myriads of Mlechchhas and barbarians, and with a vast armament of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and foot, advanced impatiently against Mathurá... wearying every day the animal that carried him, but insensible of fatigue himself'.

notes: Blends HV 1.111 (march/embassy) with VP 5.23 (origin), both present in the pack; variant_notes explicitly sanction the VP origin account. Closing 'name ran ahead like fire' is connective narration.

statements.claim: Kalayavana's host covered the plain like locusts, followed by a new river born of the urine and dung of horses and camels, named Aswasakrit.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114 (19-24): Dasyu kings 'resembling a swarm of locusts'; 'By the urine and excreta of the soldiers a river was created... passed by the name of Aswasakrit'.

statements.claim: Gargya, dishonored by his brother-in-law before the king, gave up his wife in anger and did penance on pounded iron for twelve years; Rudra conferred a boon of an all-powerful son able to discomfit the Vrishni and Andhaka descendants in battle.

The childless Yavana king heard of the boon, brought Gargya to his kingdom and consoled him; Gargya begot Kalayavana on the Apsara Gopali in the guise of a milk-woman; the boy was raised in the king's inner apartment like his own son and became king after the old king's demise.
When Kalayavana grew powerful, the Shaka, Tukhara, Darava, Parava, Tangana, Khasha, Panhava and hundreds of Mlechcha kings living near Himavan took shelter under him.

Encircled by those Dasyu kings in various dresses and weapons, the Yavana king set out for Mathura, agitating the earth with horses, elephants, asses, camels and a huge army; dust covered the sun's path.
Krishna took no notice of Kalayavana as he grew up among the Yavanas because he had heard from Narada the story of his obtaining the boon.

Krishna told his kinsmen of the calamity, that the enemy was unslayable by them because of the trident-holder's boon, that conciliation had failed, that Narada had said 'I am to live here', that Jarasandha was unforgiving and other kings, displeased at Kamsa's destruction, had sought refuge with the Magadha king and slain many Yadava kinsmen, and that they would never prosper living in the city.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114 (25-28): Krishna's address reproduced nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: Desirous of retreating, Krishna sent an envoy to Kalayavana with a sealed jar holding a highly dreadful black serpent resembling a collection of collyrium; the emissary said 'Krishna is like a deadly serpent' and showed the jar.
Kalayavana understood the Yadavas sent it to terrorize him, filled the jar with dreadful ants which devoured the serpent to ashes, and the jar was sealed anew and sent back.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114 (32-33): 'Kalayavana filled that jar with dreadful ants... serpent was eaten up by the innumerable ants... reduced to ashes. Thereupon seali[ng]...'; index excerpt confirms the counter-stratagem.

notes: Faithful to HV 1.114; uses the HV variant (Gopali/Apsara) for the birth, consistent with pack. 'King who could not be frightened' closing is connective.

statements.claim: From Girivraja the king of Magadha whirled a mace ninety-nine times and hurled it toward Mathura, where Krishna of wonderful deeds was residing.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.19: 'the mighty king of Magadha from his city of Girivraja, whirling a mace ninety-nine times, hurled it towards Mathura. At that time Krishna of wonderful deeds was residing at Mathura'.

statements.claim: An enmity arose between Jarasandha and Krishna after king Kansa was slain by Vasudeva.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.19: 'Some time after when king Kansa was slain by Vasudeva, an enmity arose between him and Krishna'.

statements.claim: Jarasandha was the son of Vrihadratha; when Chandakausika came to the Magadha country, Vrihadratha went out to receive him with ministers, priest, wives and son, offering his whole kingdom along with the boy.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.19: Krishna's narration of Chandakausika's visit and Vrihadratha's offering.

statements.claim: The sage prophesied the son would grow in prosperity and prowess, that other monarchs could never equal his energy, that weapons hurled even by celestials would cause him no pain, that he would blaze above all crowned heads and rob all monarchs of splendour, and that all kings of the earth would obey him.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.19: prophecy quoted nearly verbatim ('weapons hurled at him even by the celestials will fail to produce the least pain in him... rob all monarchs of their splendour... all the kings of the earth will live in obedience to the commands of this child').

statements.claim: Vrihadratha installed Jarasandha on the throne and, feeling distaste for worldly pleasures, retired into the woods with his two wives; Jarasandha ruled like a father and brought numerous kings under his sway.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.19: 'installed Jarasandha, on the throne... retired into the woods... ruled his kingdom like a father... brought numerous kings under his sway'.

statements.claim: The mace fell near Mathura at a distance of ninety-nine yojanas from Girivraja, at a place called Gadavasan adjacent to Mathura; the citizens informed Krishna of the fall.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.19: 'fell near Mathura at a distance of ninety-nine yojanas from Gririvraja... called Gadavasan... The citizens... went unto Krishna and informed him of the fall of the mace'.

statements.claim: Jarasandha had two supporters, Hansa and Dimvaka, incapable of being slain by weapons, foremost in the science of politics and morality, who with Jarasandha were more than a match for the three worlds.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.19: 'two supporters called Hansa and Dimvaka, both of whom were incapable of being slain by weapons... more than a match for three worlds'.

statements.claim: For that reason the Kukkura, Andhaka and Vrishni tribes, from motives of policy, never deemed it proper to fight with him.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.19: 'it was for this reason that the powerful Kukkura, Andhaka and Vrishni tribes... did not deem it proper to fight with him'.

notes: Faithful to MBh 2.19; 'iron seemed the shape of his anger' and closing warning framing are connective narration. 'Heights of Girivraja' is a minor atmospheric rephrasing of 'from his city of Girivraja'.

statements.claim: Krishna stated that both Hansa and Dimvaka had fallen and Kamsa with all his followers had been slain, so the time had come for Jarasandha's destruction.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: 'both Hansa and Dimvaka have fallen; Kansa also with all his followers has been slain. The time hath, therefore come for the destruction of Jarasandha'.

statements.claim: Jarasandha was incapable of being vanquished in battle even by all the celestials and Asuras fighting together, but could be vanquished in a personal struggle with bare arms.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: 'incapable of being vanquished in battle even by all the celestials and the Asuras (fighting together). We think, however, that he should be vanquished in a personal struggle with bare arms'.

statements.claim: Krishna said: in me is policy, in Bhima is strength, in Arjuna is triumph; as prelude to performing the Rajasuya they would achieve the destruction of the ruler of Magadha.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: quoted verbatim in the pack excerpt.

statements.claim: Krishna said that when the three approached the monarch in secret he would engage with one of them, and from fear of disgrace, covetousness and pride of strength would summon Bhima, whom death-like Bhimasena would slay.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: 'From fear of disgrace, from covetousness, and from pride of strength he will certainly summon Bhima to the encounter... the long-armed and mighty Bhimasena will effect the destruction of the king'.

statements.claim: Krishna asked Yudhishthira to make over Bhima and Arjuna to him as a pledge.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: 'then make over to me, as a pledge, Bhima and Arjuna without loss of time'.

statements.claim: Yudhishthira replied that Krishna was the lord of the Pandavas, that what he said was consistent with wise counsels, and that one under Krishna's command could regard Jarasandha as already slain, the confined monarchs freed, and the Rajasuya accomplished.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: Yudhishthira's reply quoted nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: Yudhishthira spoke of leadership: troops well led do excellent service, a leaderless force is called inert, the wise conduct water into low places, and fishermen drain tanks through holes.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: 'Troops, when properly led, always do excellent service. A force without a leader hath been called inert by the wise... Even fishermen cause the water (of tank) to run out through holes'.

statements.claim: Yudhishthira urged placing Krishna in the van — whose strength consists in wisdom and policy — with Arjuna following Krishna and Bhima following Arjuna.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: 'let, therefore, Arjuna, the son of Pritha, follow Krishna... and let Bhima follow Arjuna. Policy and good fortune and might will (then) bring about success'.

statements.claim: The trio set out for Magadha in the garb of Snataka Brahmanas, blessed by friends' and relatives' speeches, their bodies blazing like the sun, moon and fire with wrath at the sad lot of their relative kings.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: 'set out for Magadha attired in the garb of Snataka Brahmanas of resplendent bodies... inflamed with wrath at the sad lot of their relative kings, those bodies of theirs became much more blazing'.

statements.claim: The people, beholding Krishna and Arjuna, never before vanquished, with Bhima in the van, regarded Jarasandha as already slain.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: 'the people... regarded Jarasandha as already slain'.

statements.claim: Their route ran from the Kuru country through Kuru-jangala, the lake of lotuses, the Kalakuta hills, the rivers Gandaki, Sadanira and Sarkaravarta, the Sarayu, Eastern Kosala, Mithila, the Mala and Charamanwati, the Ganges and the Sone, to Magadha in the heart of Kushamva, and the hills of Goratha overlooking the city.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: full itinerary matches, including 'arrived at Magadha in the heart of (the country of) Kushamva' and 'the hills of Goratha'.

notes: Faithful to MBh 2.20; variant_notes note the BP 10.71 attribution variant but this story correctly follows the MBh attribution to Krishna. Opening 'one obstacle left' is connective framing.

statements.claim: Krishna showed Arjuna the capital of Magadha filled with flocks and herds, never-exhausted water, fine mansions in excellent array, free from every calamity.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'behold... the great capital of Magadha... Filled with flocks and herds and its stock of water never exhausted... free from every kind of calamity'.

statements.claim: Five large hills — Vaihara, Varaha, Vrishava, Rishigiri and the delightful Chaitya — of high peaks and tall cool-shaded trees, connected, with slopes concealed by fragrant flowering Lodhra forests, protected Girivraja.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: the five hills and Lodhra forests described as such.

statements.claim: Gautama of rigid vows begot Kakshivat and other celebrated sons there, and the monarchs of Anga and Vanga and other countries had come in olden times to Gautama's abode and passed their days in joy.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'the illustrious Gautama of rigid vows begat... Kakshivat and other celebrated sons... the mighty monarchs of Anga, and Vanga and other countries, came to the abode of Gautama, and passed their days in joy'.

statements.claim: Krishna said that owning such an impregnable city Jarasandha was ever bent on seeking fruition of his purposes unlike other monarchs, and that they would humble his pride by slaying him that day.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'Owning such a delightful and impregnable city, Jarasandha is ever bent on seeking the fruition of his purposes... We shall, however, by slaying him to-day humble his pride'.

statements.claim: The brothers entered the city of Magadha and approached Girivraja, full of cheerful, well-fed inhabitants of all four orders with perennial festivities.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'full of cheerful and well-fed inhabitants belonging to all the four orders, and where festivities were perennial'.

statements.claim: At the city gate the brothers, instead of passing through, pierced the heart of the high Chaityaka peak worshipped by Vrihadratha's race and the citizens, delightful to all Magadhas.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'On arriving then at the gate of the city, the brothers (instead of passing through it) began to pierce... the heart of the high Chaityaka peak'.

statements.claim: There Vrihadratha had slain the cannibal Rishava and made three drums from his hide, which when beaten sounded for a full month; at that point the brothers broke the peak down.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'Vrihadratha had slain a cannibal called Rishava... made of his hide three drums... once beaten their sound lasted one full month... the brothers broke down the Chaityaka peak... at that point where those drums... used to yield their continuous sound'.

statements.claim: Desirous of slaying Jarasandha they seemed by that act to place their feet on their foe's head, and entered the city with joyful hearts.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'desirous of slaying Jarasandha they seemed by that act of theirs to place their feet upon the head of their foe... with joyful hearts they then entered the city'.

statements.claim: The Brahmanas of Girivraja saw evil omens and reported them to Jarasandha; his priest made him mount an elephant and whirled lighted brands about him, and Jarasandha entered on a sacrifice with vows and fasts to ward off the evils.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'the learned Brahmanas residing within the city saw many evil omens... the priest making the king mount an elephant whirled lighted brands about him... entered upon the celebration of a sacrifice, with proper vows and fasts'.

statements.claim: Unarmed, with bare arms as their only weapons, the brothers entered the capital in the guise of Brahmanas, beheld the shops full of edibles and floral wreaths, snatched garlands forcibly from the flower-vendors, and passed along the public road.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'the brothers unarmed... entered the capital in the guise of Brahmanas... snatched forcibly from the flower-vendors the garlands they had exposed for sale'.

statements.claim: Decked in garlands and ear-rings, arms besmeared with sandal paste like sala trunks, they entered Jarasandha's abode like Himalayan lions; the Magadha people wondered at the elephant-like heroes, and the bulls among men passed through three crowded gates to the king.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: all similes and details match ('like Himalayan lions eyeing cattle-folds... arms... looked like the trunks of sala trees... passing through three gates that were crowded with men').

statements.claim: Jarasandha rose in haste and received them with water for the feet, honey and the Arghya ingredients, gifts of kine and other respects, saying 'Ye are welcome'; both Arjuna and Bhima remained silent.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'rising up in haste received them with water to wash their feet with, and honey and the other ingredients of the Arghya--with gifts of kine... Ye are welcome!... both Partha and Bhima remained silent at this'.

notes: Faithful to MBh 2.21. 'All his rites could not undo what the portents promised' is connective interpretation, not a factual assertion.

statements.claim: Jarasandha rose in haste and received the three Brahmanas with water to wash the feet, honey and the other Arghya ingredients, gifts of kine and other respects, saying 'Ye are welcome'.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21 (also quoted in this pack): 'rising up in haste received them with water to wash their feet with, and honey and the other ingredients of the Arghya--with gifts of kine... Ye are welcome'.

statements.claim: Both of his two younger guests (Bhima and Arjuna) remained silent.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'both Partha and Bhima remained silent at this'.

statements.claim: Jarasandha came to the meeting amid ill omens: Brahmanas of Girivraja had seen evil signs and reported them, his priest made him mount an elephant and whirled lighted brands, and he entered on a sacrifice with vows and fasts.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'the learned Brahmanas residing within the city saw many evil omens which they reported to Jarasandha... the priest making the king mount an elephant whirled lighted brands about him... entered upon the celebration of a sacrifice, with proper vows and fasts'.

statements.claim: The three strangers had passed along the public road past shops full of edibles and floral wreaths and snatched garlands from the flower-vendors; the Magadha people wondered at them, and they passed through three crowded gates to the king.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: repeated details match (shops, garlands, three gates, elephant-like heroes with sala-trunk arms).

statements.claim: Krishna spoke for the three: 'O king of kings, these two are now in the observance of a vow. Therefore they will not speak. Silent they will remain till midnight. After that hour they will speak with thee.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (MBh 2.21): 'And addressing the monarch Krishna said,--O king of kings these two are now in the observance of a vow. Therefore they will not speak. Silent they will remain till midnight After that hour they will speak with thee!'

statements.claim: Whatever questions Jarasandha might wish to ask would have to wait until the night hour.
statements.evidence: Inference from the vow-of-silence explanation; consistent with the source, not a new factual claim.

notes: Faithful to MBh 2.21; recap material repeats pack details. Closing meditation on the waiting court is connective narration.
